This proposal recommends a phased deployment of a secure internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The program will begin with targeted use cases and controlled pilots, establish the required governance and technical foundation, and expand based on demonstrated value, user feedback, and risk assessment.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, secure, and easy-to-use AI assistant that improves access to organizational knowledge and reduces time spent on routine knowledge work.

The program will pursue five related objectives. First, it will improve employee productivity by supporting tasks such as information retrieval, drafting, summarization, translation, meeting preparation, data interpretation, and workflow navigation. Second, it will make internal knowledge easier to find and use by connecting employees to approved policies, procedures, project information, and frequently asked questions through a natural-language interface. Third, it will improve consistency and service quality by providing standardized responses grounded in authoritative organizational sources. Fourth, it will establish responsible AI practices, including access controls, data protection, transparency, monitoring, human oversight, and clear acceptable-use requirements. Finally, it will create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows and business applications.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide a centrally managed AI assistant accessible through the organization’s existing collaboration and productivity environment, with browser and mobile access where appropriate. Employees will be able to use the assistant for general productivity support and, where authorized, to retrieve information from approved internal sources.

Initial capabilities will include conversational question answering over selected internal knowledge repositories; document summarization and comparison; drafting and editing of emails, reports, briefs, and other business content; meeting preparation and follow-up; translation and tone adjustment; support for internal policies and procedures; and assistance with common human resources, information technology, procurement, finance, and operational questions. The assistant will clearly distinguish between generated content and authoritative source material and will provide citations or links to source documents whenever feasible.

The first release will focus on low- and moderate-risk use cases. The assistant will not independently make employment, legal, financial, safety, security, or other high-impact decisions. It will not be permitted to disclose information beyond a user’s existing authorization, execute sensitive transactions without explicit approval, or replace required professional, managerial, or regulatory review. High-risk use cases may be considered in later phases only after separate risk assessment, controls design, and executive approval.

The project includes business process discovery, data and content readiness, platform selection or configuration, identity and access integration, security and privacy review, governance, user training, communications, pilot deployment, adoption measurement, and operational support. It does not initially include the development of fully autonomous agents, unrestricted access to all organizational data, or the replacement of existing enterprise systems.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be delivered over approximately twelve months through a staged program.

During months one and two, the organization will establish program governance, confirm business priorities, assess technical and data readiness, define acceptable-use policies, identify pilot groups, and complete an initial security, privacy, legal, and compliance assessment. The project team will select the preferred technology approach, define success measures, and document the initial risk register.

During months three and four, the team will configure the assistant, integrate enterprise identity and access management, connect a limited set of high-quality knowledge sources, and establish logging, monitoring, content-management, and incident-response processes. Representative use cases will be tested with employees and subject-matter experts. Evaluation will focus on answer accuracy, source attribution, security boundaries, usability, accessibility, and resilience against misuse.

During months five and six, the organization will conduct a controlled pilot involving approximately 300 to 500 employees from selected functions. Pilot participants will receive training and guidance on effective and responsible use. Their feedback, usage patterns, support needs, and task-level productivity impacts will inform improvements to the assistant, content sources, policies, and training materials. The pilot will proceed only after completion of agreed security and privacy gates.

During months seven through nine, the assistant will expand to approximately 1,500 employees across a broader set of business units. Additional knowledge repositories and approved use cases will be introduced incrementally. The project team will monitor adoption, response quality, incidents, employee sentiment, and measurable time savings. Business leaders will review results before approving organization-wide deployment.

During months ten through twelve, the assistant will be made available to the remaining employees, subject to readiness criteria. The final phase will include organization-wide communications, role-based training, support-model transition, performance optimization, and a post-implementation review. At the end of the first year, the organization will determine which capabilities should be scaled, redesigned, or discontinued and will establish a roadmap for the next stage of AI-enabled workflows.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

The program will be governed by an executive steering committee with representation from technology, information security, privacy, legal, compliance, human resources, communications, finance, and key business functions. A product owner and cross-functional delivery team will manage the day-to-day program.

The assistant will use the organization’s existing identity, authentication, and authorization controls. It will respect source-system permissions so that employees can retrieve only information they are already authorized to access. Data will be encrypted in transit and at rest, and organizational content will not be used to train external models unless explicitly approved under contract and policy. Retention, logging, auditability, and data residency requirements will be defined before production deployment.

The organization will publish an acceptable-use standard explaining appropriate and prohibited uses, employee responsibilities, limitations of generated content, and requirements for human review. Training will emphasize that AI-generated responses may be incomplete, inaccurate, or misleading and must be verified when used for consequential work. The organization will also establish processes for reporting harmful or incorrect responses, investigating incidents, correcting source content, and suspending capabilities when necessary.

Content owners will remain accountable for the accuracy, currency, and classification of information made available to the assistant. A formal review process will govern the onboarding of new data sources and use cases. The program will incorporate accessibility, records-management, intellectual-property, and employee-relations considerations throughout implementation.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a dedicated core team for the first twelve months, supported by part-time specialists from business functions. Core staffing should include an executive sponsor, program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, data and knowledge engineers, integration engineers, cybersecurity specialists, privacy and legal advisors, user-experience and accessibility specialists, change-management and communications leads, training specialists, support representatives, and business analysts. Subject-matter experts from participating functions will be needed to identify use cases, validate responses, curate content, and define escalation paths.

The organization will also require an approved AI platform or service, enterprise identity integration, secure connectors to selected knowledge repositories, monitoring and evaluation tools, content-management capabilities, and service-desk support. The production environment should include safeguards for prompt and response logging, access auditing, usage analytics, data-loss prevention, threat detection, and model-performance evaluation.

The budget will consist of platform licensing or consumption fees, implementation and integration services, security and compliance work, data preparation, training and communications, user support, and ongoing operations. A contingency should be reserved for additional data remediation, model or platform changes, and unforeseen security or compliance requirements. Costs should be refined during the discovery phase and evaluated against measured productivity gains and avoided support effort.

Following organization-wide launch, the assistant will require a permanent operating model. This should include product management, platform administration, content stewardship, security monitoring, model and response evaluation, user support, training updates, vendor management, and periodic governance reviews.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable employee value without compromising organizational security, privacy, or trust. Within six months of organization-wide availability, the program should achieve meaningful adoption, with at least 60 percent of employees accessing the assistant and at least 40 percent using it monthly. Adoption targets may be adjusted by function based on role relevance and access to approved use cases.

The assistant should reduce the time employees spend searching for information and completing selected routine knowledge tasks by at least 20 percent in participating use cases. Pilot and post-launch surveys should show that at least 75 percent of active users find the assistant useful and that a clear majority would recommend it for approved work activities. Business functions should document validated productivity improvements, reduced support volume, faster onboarding, improved consistency, or other quantifiable benefits.

Quality and trust will be measured through structured evaluations and user feedback. At least 90 percent of responses in designated knowledge-based use cases should be materially accurate or appropriately qualified, with source citations available where expected. High-severity privacy, security, or data-access incidents must remain at zero, and all reported incidents must be investigated within defined service-level targets. No high-impact decision or sensitive transaction may be performed without the required human authorization and review.

Operational success will also require completion of mandatory employee guidance, established ownership for all connected knowledge sources, successful access-control testing, documented incident-response procedures, and performance that meets agreed availability and response-time targets. After the first year, the steering committee will review the results and approve continued investment based on adoption, productivity impact, risk performance, employee trust, and the strength of the operating model.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization represents a practical opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to institutional knowledge, and establish responsible AI capability at enterprise scale. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly while addressing data quality, security, governance, and change-management requirements before broad expansion. With executive sponsorship, cross-functional ownership, disciplined risk controls, and clear measures of success, the program can deliver immediate benefits to employees while creating a sustainable foundation for future AI-enabled services.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a wide range of information sources, business applications, policies, and operational processes to complete their work. Relevant knowledge is often distributed across document repositories, intranets, collaboration platforms, ticketing systems, and line-of-business applications. As a result, employees spend significant time searching for information, repeating routine tasks, drafting content, and requesting assistance from subject-matter experts.

Advances in enterprise artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, centrally governed AI assistant that can help them find trusted information, summarize documents, draft and revise content, answer questions about internal policies and procedures, and support selected workflow activities. A properly designed internal assistant can improve productivity while maintaining appropriate controls for privacy, security, regulatory compliance, intellectual property, and human decision-making.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for all employees, beginning with targeted use cases and expanding based on measured value, user feedback, and risk assessments. The assistant will be integrated with approved enterprise knowledge sources and collaboration tools, while access to information will remain governed by existing identity, authorization, and data-classification controls.

## Objectives

The project will establish a secure, useful, and scalable AI capability that improves how employees access knowledge and complete routine work. The primary objective is to reduce the time employees spend searching for information, preparing standard documents, and performing repetitive knowledge-work tasks. The assistant will provide timely responses grounded in approved internal sources and will clearly identify when information is uncertain, unavailable, or requires human review.

A second objective is to improve consistency and quality across common business activities, including policy interpretation, onboarding, customer and employee communications, meeting preparation, research, reporting, and knowledge management. The assistant will support employees rather than replace professional judgment, and it will not independently make high-impact decisions involving employment, legal matters, financial commitments, safety, or regulatory obligations.

The project will also establish the organization’s long-term operating model for responsible AI. This will include governance, security standards, data-access controls, usage policies, training, monitoring, vendor management, and a process for approving future AI use cases.

## Scope

The initial solution will be an enterprise conversational assistant accessible through approved web, desktop, and collaboration-platform interfaces. It will support natural-language questions, document summarization, drafting, rewriting, translation, information extraction, brainstorming, and guided completion of selected internal processes. Where appropriate, the assistant will provide links or citations to the source material used to generate its response.

The assistant will initially connect to high-value, well-governed information sources such as approved policies, procedures, employee handbooks, knowledge bases, standard operating procedures, training materials, and selected project or departmental repositories. Integration with additional systems will occur only after data quality, authorization, retention, and security requirements have been assessed. The system will respect existing role-based access permissions and will not expose information merely because it is available somewhere within the enterprise.

The scope includes platform selection or configuration, identity and access integration, knowledge-source preparation, security and privacy review, user experience design, pilot deployment, employee training, communications, support procedures, usage monitoring, and post-launch improvement. It also includes the development of a responsible-use policy and a governance process for evaluating new use cases.

The initial scope excludes fully autonomous action in critical business systems, unrestricted access to confidential or regulated data, automated employment or financial decisions, and use cases that require the assistant to act without human confirmation. Such capabilities may be considered in later phases following separate risk assessments, technical validation, and executive approval.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be completed through a phased program lasting approximately twelve months, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During the first six weeks, the project team will establish governance, confirm business priorities, document technical and regulatory requirements, assess available platforms, and identify the initial use cases. The team will also conduct a baseline assessment of current search, support, and knowledge-management activities so that improvements can be measured against existing performance.

From weeks seven through fourteen, the organization will configure the selected AI platform and prepare the initial knowledge sources. This phase will include identity and access integration, data classification, content quality review, retrieval and response testing, security controls, logging, retention settings, and evaluation against representative employee questions. A cross-functional governance group will approve the initial use cases and launch criteria.

From months four through six, the organization will conduct a controlled pilot involving approximately 300 to 500 employees from a representative mix of functions, locations, and levels of technical familiarity. Pilot users will receive training and clear guidance on appropriate use. The project team will monitor answer quality, source attribution, security behavior, adoption, user satisfaction, and operational impact. Feedback will be used to improve prompts, knowledge sources, workflows, and support materials.

From months seven through nine, the assistant will expand to approximately 1,500 employees across additional business functions. This stage will validate the platform at greater scale, test support and operating procedures, and introduce approved integrations with collaboration and productivity tools. The organization will conduct a formal readiness review before proceeding to enterprise deployment.

From months ten through twelve, the assistant will be made available to the remaining employees through a managed rollout. Communications, role-based training, manager briefings, office hours, and help-desk support will accompany the launch. Usage and risk metrics will be reviewed weekly during the initial deployment period and monthly thereafter.

After the first year, the program will enter an optimization phase focused on improving knowledge coverage, retiring low-value use cases, expanding high-performing workflows, and incorporating new capabilities under the established governance model.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship from a senior leader with authority across technology, operations, risk, and business functions. A product owner will be accountable for the roadmap, prioritization, budget, and business outcomes. A program manager will coordinate delivery across technical, legal, security, communications, and operational teams.

The core delivery team should include enterprise architects, AI and data engineers, identity and access specialists, information-security professionals, privacy and legal representatives, knowledge-management specialists, user-experience designers, change-management and communications leads, learning and development staff, and service-desk representatives. Business subject-matter experts from participating functions will be needed to validate content, define use cases, test responses, and establish acceptable operating procedures.

During implementation, the organization should plan for a core team of approximately 12 to 18 full-time equivalent personnel, supplemented by part-time contributors from business units and external specialists where necessary. After deployment, ongoing operations will typically require a smaller permanent team responsible for product management, platform administration, knowledge curation, model and prompt evaluation, security monitoring, user support, governance, and continuous improvement.

The technology budget will cover platform licensing or cloud consumption, integration and development, identity and security controls, monitoring and evaluation tools, data preparation, training, change management, and contingency costs. The organization should establish usage limits and cost-monitoring controls before broad deployment, with particular attention to high-volume users, automated workloads, and advanced model capabilities.

## Governance, Security, and Risk Management

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework approved before the pilot begins. The framework will define permitted and prohibited uses, data-handling requirements, human-review obligations, records-management expectations, incident-reporting procedures, and accountability for business outcomes.

Access will be managed through the organization’s existing identity provider and authorization model. The assistant will retrieve information only from sources the individual user is already permitted to access. Sensitive information will be subject to additional controls, including data-loss prevention, encryption, audit logging, retention policies, and, where appropriate, exclusion from the initial deployment.

Responses will be evaluated for accuracy, relevance, harmful content, bias, confidentiality leakage, and inappropriate confidence. The assistant will be configured to acknowledge uncertainty and direct users to authoritative sources or human experts when appropriate. Employees will be informed that AI-generated content must be reviewed before it is used in external communications, official records, regulated activities, or consequential decisions.

The organization will maintain a clear process for reporting inaccurate answers, privacy concerns, security incidents, and harmful outputs. All significant incidents will be investigated, documented, and used to improve system controls and training.

## Success Criteria

The program will be considered successful if it demonstrates measurable productivity gains without compromising security, privacy, or trust. Within six months of enterprise deployment, at least 60 percent of eligible employees should have used the assistant, with at least 35 percent using it monthly. Adoption targets may be adjusted by function based on the relevance of available use cases.

For the initial use cases, the organization should target a 20 percent reduction in time spent locating internal information and a 15 percent reduction in time spent completing selected drafting, summarization, and routine research activities. At least 80 percent of pilot users should report that the assistant helps them complete work more efficiently, and at least 75 percent should indicate that they understand when human review is required.

Response-quality evaluations should show that at least 85 percent of answers to approved knowledge questions are factually correct, relevant, and supported by appropriate source references. Critical security and privacy incidents must remain at zero, and all identified high-severity issues must have documented remediation plans before expansion to the next phase. The program should also demonstrate sustainable operating costs, defined support performance, and compliance with applicable legal, regulatory, and internal-control requirements.

Finally, success will be measured by the organization’s ability to operate and improve the assistant responsibly. This includes an active governance process, trained employees, reliable monitoring, clear ownership of knowledge sources, and a repeatable method for approving additional use cases. The intended outcome is not simply the introduction of a new technology, but the establishment of a trusted enterprise capability that enables employees to work more effectively while preserving human accountability and organizational standards.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing volume of policies, procedures, technical documentation, business data, and institutional knowledge to perform their work. Much of this information is distributed across intranet pages, document repositories, collaboration platforms, ticketing systems, and departmental applications. Employees often spend significant time searching for answers, interpreting policies, drafting routine communications, summarizing information, and completing repetitive knowledge-work tasks.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, organization-specific assistant that can retrieve approved internal information, generate drafts, summarize content, answer questions, and support common workflows. Deploying such a capability would improve productivity while preserving organizational controls around privacy, security, records management, and responsible use of AI.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an internal AI assistant available to all employees through approved enterprise channels. The assistant would be designed as a secure, governed service that augments employees rather than replaces professional judgment. It would provide reliable access to organizational knowledge, support routine work, and create a foundation for future AI-enabled business processes.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide every employee with a trusted AI assistant that can help them find information, complete routine knowledge tasks, and work more efficiently. The assistant will support natural-language interaction and, where appropriate, connect to approved internal systems and content repositories.

The deployment will pursue five related objectives. First, it will reduce the time employees spend searching for information and preparing routine documents, summaries, analyses, and communications. Second, it will improve consistency by directing employees to current, approved policies and procedures. Third, it will increase access to organizational knowledge across departments and locations. Fourth, it will establish an enterprise governance model for the safe, ethical, and compliant use of AI. Finally, it will create a scalable platform that can support future use cases, including workflow automation, service-desk assistance, employee self-service, and decision support.

The assistant will be positioned as a productivity and knowledge-management capability. It will not make autonomous employment, financial, legal, medical, safety, or other high-impact decisions. Outputs will be clearly identified as AI-generated and will require appropriate human review before being used in consequential activities.

## Scope

The initial program will deliver a secure enterprise AI assistant for all 5,000 employees, with access managed through the organization’s existing identity and access-management platform. The assistant will be available through a browser-based interface and, where supported by enterprise platforms, through approved collaboration tools and productivity applications.

Core capabilities will include question answering over approved internal content, source-linked retrieval, document summarization, drafting and editing, meeting and notes assistance, translation, brainstorming, structured data extraction, and assistance with common employee-support questions. The assistant will be configured to distinguish between public enterprise content, restricted departmental information, confidential material, and content that must not be processed. Responses will respect the user’s existing permissions, and the system will not expose information simply because it is available somewhere in the organization.

The initial knowledge sources will include selected policies, procedures, employee guidance, operational documentation, service catalogs, frequently asked questions, and other high-value content that has an identified owner and review cycle. Content will be assessed, cleaned, classified, and indexed before being made available to the assistant. Source citations and links will be included wherever technically feasible so employees can verify responses and access authoritative material.

The program will also include a limited number of integrations with high-value systems, such as the intranet, document-management platform, collaboration environment, service desk, and learning or human-resources knowledge bases. Integrations that permit the assistant to take actions on behalf of users—such as submitting requests, updating records, or initiating workflows—will be introduced only after security, approval, audit, and rollback controls are established.

The scope includes platform selection or configuration, security architecture, content preparation, identity integration, governance, user training, communications, pilot deployment, enterprise rollout, support processes, and measurement. It does not initially include fully autonomous agents, unrestricted access to all organizational data, automated decisions affecting employees or customers, or replacement of existing systems of record.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program will be delivered over approximately twelve months through controlled phases, followed by ongoing optimization.

During months one and two, the organization will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint a product owner, define governance and risk controls, identify priority use cases, inventory potential data sources, and establish baseline measures for productivity, search effort, employee satisfaction, and support demand. The team will also evaluate the organization’s existing technology landscape and select the preferred AI platform or implementation approach.

During months three and four, the program will focus on architecture and preparation. The delivery team will configure identity and access controls, data-loss prevention, logging, retention, monitoring, and environment separation. Priority content will be reviewed for ownership, accuracy, classification, duplication, and currency. Initial security, privacy, legal, records-management, and accessibility assessments will be completed. A small set of high-value use cases will be developed using representative but controlled data.

During months five and six, the organization will conduct a pilot with approximately 200 to 300 employees drawn from different departments, roles, and levels of technical familiarity. Pilot participants will receive training and clear usage guidance. The team will measure answer quality, source accuracy, adoption, time savings, user satisfaction, security events, and support requirements. Feedback will be used to refine prompts, retrieval behavior, content controls, user experience, and operating procedures.

During months seven and eight, the assistant will enter a controlled expansion phase involving approximately 1,000 employees. Additional knowledge sources and selected integrations will be introduced following the same approval process. Departmental champions will be trained to support adoption, identify new use cases, and report issues. The program will conduct a formal readiness review covering performance, risk, accessibility, support capacity, and governance compliance.

During months nine through twelve, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining workforce in waves. Communications will explain the assistant’s capabilities, limitations, acceptable-use requirements, and methods for reporting inaccurate or unsafe responses. Adoption will be monitored by department and use case, and additional training will be provided where utilization or confidence is low. At the end of the first year, the organization will complete a benefits review and approve the next phase of integrations, automation, and capability expansion.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework overseen by a cross-functional steering group representing information technology, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, records management, human resources, risk, accessibility, communications, and business leadership. The steering group will approve use cases, define risk classifications, review incidents, and authorize access to sensitive data or action-taking capabilities.

Security controls will include single sign-on, role- and attribute-based access, encryption in transit and at rest, environment segregation, detailed audit logging, vulnerability management, security testing, and continuous monitoring. Prompts and responses will be handled according to the organization’s data-classification requirements. The service will be configured so that organizational data is not used to train a public model without explicit authorization. Sensitive information, including credentials, regulated personal data, and confidential third-party information, will be subject to appropriate restrictions.

The assistant will provide citations or links to source material where possible, communicate uncertainty when evidence is incomplete, and enable users to report inaccurate, inappropriate, or potentially harmful responses. High-impact decisions will remain under human control. Employees will receive clear guidance not to treat AI-generated content as authoritative without verification, particularly in legal, financial, employment, safety, security, and customer-impacting contexts.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a dedicated cross-functional team during implementation and a smaller permanent operating team after launch. Core implementation staffing should include an executive sponsor, a product owner, a program or project manager, an enterprise architect, two to three AI or machine-learning engineers, two data and content engineers, one or two integration engineers, a cybersecurity specialist, a privacy and compliance lead, a user-experience or service-design lead, a change-management lead, a training and communications specialist, and representatives from legal, records management, accessibility, and business operations. Departments participating in the pilot should provide subject-matter experts and content owners on a part-time basis.

After rollout, the operating model should retain a product owner, platform and AI engineers, a content and knowledge-management team, a security and compliance function, a support lead, and a network of departmental champions. A service desk process should be established for access issues, technical problems, content corrections, and suspected policy violations. Content owners will be accountable for maintaining the accuracy and review cycle of information made available to the assistant.

The program will require an enterprise AI platform or equivalent technology, secure cloud or approved hosting capacity, identity and access integration, data connectors, content-indexing capabilities, observability and evaluation tools, security controls, user-support tools, and training materials. The budget should include licensing or consumption costs, implementation services where needed, data preparation, integration work, security and privacy assessment, change management, training, and ongoing operations. A contingency should be reserved for increased usage, additional data remediation, and unplanned integration or compliance requirements.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees through approved channels, operates within documented security and governance controls, and demonstrates measurable value in priority use cases.

Within six months of enterprise rollout, the program should achieve meaningful adoption, with a target of at least 60 percent of employees using the assistant at least once and at least 35 percent using it monthly. At least 80 percent of pilot and early-adopter users should report that the assistant saves time or improves access to information. For selected use cases, the organization should target a 20 percent reduction in time spent searching for internal information and a 15 percent reduction in time spent completing routine drafting, summarization, and knowledge tasks.

Quality targets should include at least 90 percent accuracy for responses grounded in approved enterprise content during formal evaluation, with source citations available for the large majority of knowledge-management responses. Content owners should resolve reported inaccuracies within defined service levels, and no critical security or privacy incident should result from uncontrolled access or unauthorized use of organizational data.

Operational success will also be measured through system availability, response time, support-ticket volume, training completion, accessibility compliance, and the number of approved use cases adopted by departments. The program will conduct quarterly reviews of usage, benefits, risks, incidents, content quality, and employee feedback. Expansion into workflow automation or sensitive data domains will occur only when the relevant controls and business benefits have been demonstrated.

## Conclusion

A secure internal AI assistant can provide immediate value across a 5,000-employee organization by making trusted knowledge easier to access and reducing the effort required for routine knowledge work. A phased deployment will allow the organization to establish strong controls, validate benefits, improve content quality, and build employee confidence before expanding into more advanced capabilities.

With executive sponsorship, disciplined governance, appropriate technical investment, and sustained attention to training and content management, the organization can create a practical AI service that improves productivity while protecting privacy, security, and professional accountability. This proposal recommends proceeding with the twelve-month program and beginning the foundation phase immediately.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a broad and growing range of information, systems, and processes to perform their work. Policies, procedures, project documentation, knowledge bases, reports, and operational data are often distributed across collaboration platforms, document repositories, business applications, and individual teams. As a result, employees spend significant time searching for information, interpreting internal guidance, preparing routine content, and responding to recurring questions.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence create an opportunity to improve this experience through a secure internal AI assistant. The proposed assistant would provide employees with a single, conversational interface for finding approved organizational information, summarizing documents, drafting routine content, answering policy and process questions, and supporting selected workflow activities. The assistant would be designed to operate within the organization’s existing security, privacy, identity, and records-management frameworks.

The initiative is intended to augment employees rather than replace professional judgment or decision-making. It will focus on reducing administrative effort, improving access to institutional knowledge, increasing consistency in routine work, and establishing a responsible foundation for future AI-enabled services.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to deploy a trusted internal AI assistant that is available to employees through the organization’s existing digital workplace environment and capable of delivering useful, secure, and appropriately governed support.

The initiative will pursue the following outcomes:

- Enable employees to locate and understand approved internal information more quickly.
- Reduce time spent on repetitive research, drafting, summarization, and administrative tasks.
- Improve consistency in the use and interpretation of organizational policies, procedures, and standards.
- Provide controlled access to relevant knowledge while respecting existing user permissions and confidentiality requirements.
- Establish governance for responsible AI use, including privacy, security, transparency, human oversight, and content ownership.
- Create a scalable technical and operational foundation for future AI applications.
- Build employee confidence and capability through training, communication, and practical guidance.

## Scope

The initial program will provide a centrally managed AI assistant accessible to all employees, subject to role-based controls and acceptable-use requirements. The assistant will support conversational question answering over approved internal content, document summarization, information comparison, drafting of non-final communications and documents, meeting and project support, and guided navigation of internal services and processes.

The first release will prioritize high-value, lower-risk use cases such as human resources policies, information technology support, procurement guidance, finance procedures, workplace services, project documentation, and enterprise-wide communications. Content will be drawn from designated systems of record and connected through controlled interfaces or approved retrieval mechanisms. The assistant will cite or link to source material wherever practical so that users can verify responses.

The deployment will include integration with the organization’s identity and access-management platform, collaboration tools, document repositories, service-management systems, and selected knowledge bases. Access to content will follow existing permissions; the assistant will not be permitted to expose information that a user could not access directly through the source system.

The program will also establish an AI governance model covering data classification, privacy impact assessment, security testing, model and vendor oversight, retention, audit logging, incident response, content ownership, accessibility, and acceptable use. Employees will receive clear guidance that AI-generated responses may be incomplete or incorrect and must be reviewed before being used in consequential decisions or external communications.

The initial scope will not include fully autonomous decision-making, employment decisions, legal advice, medical advice, unrestricted access to confidential repositories, or automated actions that create material financial, operational, or reputational risk. Any future expansion into these areas will require separate assessment and approval.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program will be delivered over approximately twelve months through a sequence of controlled phases.

During months one and two, the organization will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint product and technical leadership, define governance and risk controls, identify priority use cases, inventory candidate information sources, assess data quality, select the technology approach, and complete initial privacy and security reviews. Employee representatives and business stakeholders will participate in discovery sessions to ensure that the assistant addresses real work patterns and accessibility needs.

During months three and four, the team will design and build the minimum viable service. This work will include configuring the AI platform, integrating identity and access controls, connecting a limited set of high-quality knowledge sources, establishing citation and feedback capabilities, implementing monitoring and audit logging, and developing the employee experience. A small group of approximately 100 to 150 employees from representative business areas will participate in an internal alpha.

During months five and six, the assistant will enter a controlled pilot with approximately 500 employees. Pilot participants will receive training and will be asked to evaluate response quality, usefulness, trust, ease of use, and time saved. The project team will use pilot results to improve retrieval quality, refine prompts and guardrails, address content gaps, and validate operational support processes. No broader rollout will occur until agreed security, privacy, quality, and usability thresholds have been met.

During months seven through nine, the service will be expanded to approximately 1,500 to 2,000 employees across all major functions. Additional approved content sources and use cases will be introduced in waves. Communications, training, office hours, and local business champions will support adoption. Performance, accuracy, access-control behavior, and user feedback will be reviewed continuously.

During months ten through twelve, the organization will complete the enterprise rollout to the remaining employees, subject to readiness assessments for each business area. The final phase will formalize ongoing service ownership, establish a regular model and content review cycle, evaluate benefits against the baseline, and produce a roadmap for future capabilities and integrations.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a cross-functional team supported by executive sponsorship and business ownership. During implementation, the core team is expected to include a program director, product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, software and integration engineers, data and knowledge-management specialists, cybersecurity and privacy professionals, user-experience and accessibility specialists, change-management and training leads, business analysts, quality-assurance staff, and service-support personnel.

A core implementation team of approximately 15 to 25 full-time equivalent staff is expected during the build and pilot phases, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts from participating business units. Once the service is fully deployed, ongoing operations are expected to require approximately 8 to 15 full-time equivalent staff, depending on the number of integrations, support volume, content domains, and service-level commitments.

The budget will include AI platform or model-usage costs, cloud or infrastructure services, integration and development work, security and privacy assessments, data preparation and knowledge-management activities, accessibility testing, employee training, communications, user support, monitoring, and contingency funding. A detailed financial estimate will be developed during the foundation phase after the preferred technology approach and integration requirements have been confirmed.

Each participating business unit will identify a content owner responsible for the accuracy, currency, classification, and approval of information made available to the assistant. Business units will also designate local champions to support adoption, collect feedback, and encourage responsible use. Legal, privacy, cybersecurity, records-management, human resources, and employee-representative stakeholders will participate in governance and review activities.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework approved before pilot launch. The framework will define permitted and prohibited uses, data-handling requirements, user responsibilities, escalation procedures, vendor obligations, testing standards, and accountability for business outcomes.

Security controls will include single sign-on, role-based access, encryption, secure integration patterns, environment separation, vulnerability management, audit logging, monitoring for misuse, and formal incident-response procedures. Where external AI services are used, contracts and technical controls will prevent organizational data from being used for unauthorized model training or retained beyond approved requirements.

The assistant will present appropriate notices regarding its capabilities and limitations. Responses will be grounded in approved sources where possible, and users will be encouraged to review citations and verify important information. High-impact decisions will remain subject to qualified human review. The program will also monitor for inaccurate, biased, inappropriate, or discriminatory outputs and will provide mechanisms for employees to report problematic responses.

Content quality will be managed as an ongoing business responsibility rather than treated solely as a technology issue. Source owners will maintain authoritative documents, retire obsolete content, and resolve conflicting guidance. The service team will monitor response quality and update configurations, integrations, and controls as the organization’s needs evolve.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable value, appropriate adoption, and reliable governance. Target measures will be finalized during the foundation phase, with an initial expectation that:

- At least 60 percent of employees will access the assistant within six months of enterprise rollout, with sustained monthly use by at least 35 percent of employees.
- At least 70 percent of surveyed users will report that the assistant helps them complete selected tasks more efficiently.
- Users will report an average time reduction of at least 20 percent for priority activities such as information retrieval, summarization, and routine drafting.
- At least 80 percent of evaluated responses in approved use cases will be judged useful and materially accurate, with source links available for the large majority of knowledge-based answers.
- Access-control testing will demonstrate that the assistant does not disclose content beyond a user’s authorized permissions.
- Security, privacy, accessibility, and records-management reviews will be completed before enterprise launch, with no unresolved high-risk findings.
- Employee support requests and recurring internal questions will decline in the initial priority domains, or demonstrate measurable improvement in resolution time.
- Business units will maintain named content owners and meet agreed standards for source accuracy and currency.
- The organization will establish a sustainable operating model, including service ownership, monitoring, governance reviews, user support, and a funded roadmap for future enhancements.

Success will ultimately be measured not by usage alone, but by whether the assistant becomes a trusted and responsible part of the organization’s digital workplace. The proposed phased approach will allow the organization to realize early benefits while learning from employees, managing risk, and building the capabilities required for long-term AI adoption.
